plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 18: Representative Metals, Metalloids, and Nonmetals
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a ball-and-stick model of one tetraphosphorus trisulfide molecule, P4S3, drawn against a plain white background with no axes or scale. Four orange spheres labeled "P" and three smaller yellow spheres labeled "S" are joined by cylindrical bonds colored in halves, orange on the phosphorus end and yellow on the sulfur end. Three phosphorus atoms form a triangular base across the lower part of the model, drawn in perspective with one sphere at the left, one at the right, and one nearer the viewer at the bottom center; solid orange bonds connect all three directly to one another. A fourth phosphorus sits alone at the apex. Each sulfur bridges that apical phosphorus down to one basal phosphorus, placing the sulfurs at the left, right, and middle of the model, the central one drawn in front with its bond running straight down to the near basal atom. The whole is a closed cage in which every sulfur is two-coordinate and every phosphorus three-coordinate. Splitting each bond into two colors keeps the phosphorus-sulfur links distinct and leaves the three phosphorus-phosphorus bonds around the base unmistakable — direct P-P bonding of the kind that gives phosphorus an oxidation state unusual for a group 15 element.

elements: one orange phosphorus sphere at the apex (top of cage)
three orange phosphorus spheres forming the triangular base: left, right, and front-center (nearer the viewer, appearing lower on screen)
three yellow sulfur spheres, smaller than the P spheres, at left, right, and center of the cage, each bridging the apical P to one basal P
three solid-orange cylindrical P–P bonds directly connecting the basal phosphorus atoms into a triangle
six two-tone P–S bonds (orange half on the phosphorus end, yellow half on the sulfur end): each sulfur links the apex P down to one basal P
bold black 'P' labels on each orange sphere
bold black 'S' labels on each yellow sphere
plain white background, no axes or scale

interactions.teaches: Rotating the model reveals that P4S3 is a closed 3D cage with three-fold symmetry — a triangular P3 base, a lone apical P, and three sulfurs wrapped around the waist — rather than a flat arrangement

Clicking any bond highlights every bond of that class: the three all-orange base bonds show direct phosphorus–phosphorus bonding, while the six two-tone bridges are phosphorus–sulfur links — the two bonding modes coexist in one molecule

interactions.label: Labels
interactions.teaches: Switching labels to coordination numbers lets the learner verify each sulfur touches exactly two atoms (two-coordinate) while each phosphorus touches exactly three (three-coordinate), explaining the 4:3 stoichiometry

demo_steps.title: Atom-symbol view
demo_steps.narration: The default model shows four orange P and three yellow S atoms. Click any bond: clicking an all-orange base bond lights up all three P–P bonds; clicking a two-tone bridge lights up all six P–S links. Click empty space to clear.

demo_steps.title: Coordination-number view
demo_steps.narration: Labels switch to coordination numbers: every sulfur reads 2 and every phosphorus reads 3. Three two-coordinate sulfurs bridge the apical P to the three-coordinate basal P atoms, closing the cage.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units roughly Ångström-scaled. C3v cage with the 3-fold axis along +Y (screen-up) and +Z toward the viewer. Apical P at (0, 2.05, 0). Basal P's in the y=0 plane on a circle of radius 1.27: front P at (0, 0, 1.30) — nearest the viewer so it renders lower-center and largest; left P at (-1.13, 0, -0.65); right P at (1.13, 0, -0.65). Basal P–P edge length ≈ 2.25; connect all three pairs with solid-orange cylinders (radius 0.085) to make the base triangle. Sulfurs sit just outside the lines joining apex to each basal P: front S at (0, 1.05, 0.85) (its lower bond runs nearly straight down to the front basal P, matching the source), left S at (-0.83, 1.00, -0.48), right S at (0.83, 1.00, -0.48); each S connects to the apex P and to its basal P, giving six P–S bonds of length ≈ 1.1–1.3. P spheres radius 0.36, orange #e8722a with lighter highlight #f7a54e; S spheres radius 0.28, yellow #e6dd3f with highlight #f5ee70. Every P–S bond cylinder is split at its midpoint: orange segment toward P, yellow segment toward S. Labels: bold black text ('P'/'S', or '3'/'2' in coordination mode) as camera-facing sprites centered on each sphere. Overall model spans about x ∈ [-1.6, 1.6], y ∈ [-0.4, 2.5], z ∈ [-1.1, 1.7].
interactionPlan.notes: Standard ball-and-stick: SphereGeometry with a radial-gradient look (MeshStandardMaterial plus a subtle top-left point light) to mimic the glossy spheres in the source; bonds as CylinderGeometry oriented between atom pairs, each P–S bond built from two half-length cylinders colored separately. Raycast on bond cylinders for the click interaction: store a bondClass ('PP' or 'PS') per cylinder; on click, raise emissive and slightly thicken all cylinders sharing that class while dimming the others; clicking background resets. Implement labels as CanvasTexture sprites so the toggle only swaps sprite textures ('P'/'S' ↔ '3'/'2') without touching geometry. Gentle idle is unnecessary — orbit plus click raycasting suffice.

authoredContext:
The phosphorus distills out of the furnace and is condensed into a solid or burned to form P4O10. The preparation of many other phosphorus compounds begins with P4O10. The acids and phosphates are useful as fertilizers and in the chemical industry. Other uses are in the manufacture of special alloys such as ferrophosphorus and phosphor bronze. Phosphorus is important in making pesticides, matches, and some plastics. Phosphorus is an active nonmetal. In compounds, phosphorus usually occurs in oxidation states of 3−, 3+, and 5+. Phosphorus exhibits oxidation numbers that are unusual for a group 15 element in compounds that contain phosphorus-phosphorus bonds; examples include diphosphorus tetrahydride, H2P-PH2, and tetraphosphorus trisulfide, P4S3, illustrated in the figure.

P4S3 is a component of the heads of strike-anywhere matches.

A ball-and-stick model is shown. Three orange atoms labeled “P” are single bonded together in a triangle shape. Each “P” is single bonded to yellow atoms labeled “S,” which are each single bonded to one other orange atom labeled “P.”

discrepancies: The central S atom sits noticeably lower relative to the apex P–basal P axis than in the source, slightly altering the cage's proportions
Bonds in the source are thicker and glossier with stronger specular shading; the generated bonds are thinner and flatter in appearance

In the source the two-tone P–S bond color split aligns so yellow meets the S sphere and orange meets P; the generated half-cylinder split at the midpoint is a reasonable but slightly less polished match
evaluation.notes: A faithful P4S3 cage with correct atom count, connectivity, two-tone P–S bonds, and on-sphere labels; label-mode toggle and bond-class click highlighting add real pedagogical value, with only minor proportional/shading differences from the source.
action_items: Raise the S atoms slightly (closer to the apex–base midpoint) to better match the source cage proportions
Increase bond cylinder radius and glossiness to match the source's thicker, shinier bonds
